title: The substitution model: small-step and big-step evaluation
body: The substitution model says what a program means by rewriting it. To evaluate `let x = v in e` once `v` is a value, replace every free occurrence of `x` in `e` by `v` and carry on. A *small-step* semantics does one rewrite at a time, `e -> e'`, until a value remains. A *big-step* semantics jumps straight to the answer, `e ==> v`. Both define the same results, and a small-step trace is a useful picture of what the program does.

Substitution must respect scope. A binding `let x = ...` inside the expression shadows the outer `x`, so the substitution function stops replacing under a binder for the same name. Because only closed values are substituted here, variable capture cannot happen; in a language with functions, substituting open terms needs renaming to avoid it, which is what makes the environment model attractive.

An expression that is not a value and cannot step is *stuck*, for example adding an integer to a boolean. Stuck terms are exactly the ones a type checker should reject, which is the connection to the next lessons: a type system promises that well-typed programs never get stuck.
code:
type op = Add | Mul | Le

type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Bool of bool
  | Var of string
  | Binop of op * expr * expr
  | If of expr * expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr

let is_value = function Int _ | Bool _ -> true | _ -> false

(* subst e v x is e with the value v substituted for the free variable x *)
let rec subst e v x =
  match e with
  | Var y -> if x = y then v else e
  | Int _ | Bool _ -> e
  | Binop (o, a, b) -> Binop (o, subst a v x, subst b v x)
  | If (c, t, f) -> If (subst c v x, subst t v x, subst f v x)
  | Let (y, e1, e2) ->
      let e1' = subst e1 v x in
      if x = y then Let (y, e1', e2) else Let (y, e1', subst e2 v x)

let rec step = function
  | Binop (Add, Int a, Int b) -> Int (a + b)
  | Binop (Mul, Int a, Int b) -> Int (a * b)
  | Binop (Le, Int a, Int b) -> Bool (a <= b)
  | Binop (o, e1, e2) when is_value e1 -> Binop (o, e1, step e2)
  | Binop (o, e1, e2) -> Binop (o, step e1, e2)
  | If (Bool true, t, _) -> t
  | If (Bool false, _, f) -> f
  | If (c, t, f) -> If (step c, t, f)
  | Let (x, e1, e2) when is_value e1 -> subst e2 e1 x
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> Let (x, step e1, e2)
  | Int _ | Bool _ | Var _ -> failwith "stuck"

let rec eval_small e = if is_value e then e else eval_small (step e)
let rec steps e n = if is_value e then n else steps (step e) (n + 1)

let rec eval_big = function
  | (Int _ | Bool _) as v -> v
  | Var x -> failwith ("unbound " ^ x)
  | Binop (o, a, b) -> (
      let x = eval_big a in
      let y = eval_big b in
      match (o, x, y) with
      | Add, Int x, Int y -> Int (x + y)
      | Mul, Int x, Int y -> Int (x * y)
      | Le, Int x, Int y -> Bool (x <= y)
      | _ -> failwith "stuck")
  | If (c, t, f) -> (
      match eval_big c with Bool true -> eval_big t | Bool false -> eval_big f | _ -> failwith "stuck")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval_big (subst e2 (eval_big e1) x)

let show = function Int n -> string_of_int n | Bool b -> string_of_bool b | _ -> "<expr>"

let () =
  let prog =
    Let ("x", Int 5,
         Let ("y", Binop (Mul, Var "x", Int 2),
              If (Binop (Le, Var "y", Int 10), Binop (Add, Var "y", Int 1), Int 0)))
  in
  Printf.printf "%s %s\n" (show (eval_small prog)) (show (eval_big prog));
  Printf.printf "%d steps\n" (steps prog 0);
  let shadow = Let ("x", Int 1, Let ("x", Int 2, Var "x")) in
  Printf.printf "shadowing: %s %s\n" (show (eval_small shadow)) (show (eval_big shadow));
  try ignore (eval_small (Binop (Add, Int 1, Bool true))) with Failure m -> print_endline m
challenge: Add a `Neg` constructor taking an expression, extend `step`, `eval_big` and `subst`, and print the value of `Let ("x", Int 4, Neg (Var "x"))` with both evaluators.
solution:
type expr = Int of int | Var of string | Neg of expr | Let of string * expr * expr

let is_value = function Int _ -> true | _ -> false

let rec subst e v x =
  match e with
  | Var y -> if x = y then v else e
  | Int _ -> e
  | Neg a -> Neg (subst a v x)
  | Let (y, e1, e2) ->
      let e1' = subst e1 v x in
      if x = y then Let (y, e1', e2) else Let (y, e1', subst e2 v x)

let rec step = function
  | Neg (Int n) -> Int (-n)
  | Neg e -> Neg (step e)
  | Let (x, e1, e2) when is_value e1 -> subst e2 e1 x
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> Let (x, step e1, e2)
  | Int _ | Var _ -> failwith "stuck"

let rec eval_small e = if is_value e then e else eval_small (step e)

let rec eval_big = function
  | Int n -> n
  | Var x -> failwith ("unbound " ^ x)
  | Neg e -> - eval_big e
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval_big (subst e2 (Int (eval_big e1)) x)

let () =
  let p = Let ("x", Int 4, Neg (Var "x")) in
  (match eval_small p with Int n -> Printf.printf "%d %d\n" n (eval_big p) | _ -> ())
question: What does the substitution function do when it meets `let x = ... in body` and the name being replaced is also `x`?
correct: It substitutes in the bound expression but leaves the body alone, because the inner x shadows the outer one
wrong: It substitutes everywhere, including the body
It raises an error because the name is already bound
reasoning: The inner binder introduces a new variable with the same name, so occurrences in the body no longer refer to the variable being replaced.

title: The environment model, closures and lexical scope
body: Substituting into a program is conceptually clean but inefficient, since each binding rewrites the whole body. The environment model keeps the body as it is and carries a table from names to values. Looking a variable up consults the table, and `let x = e1 in e2` evaluates `e2` in the table extended with `x`.

Functions make the choice of table matter. A *closure* pairs a function with the environment where it was defined, and calling it evaluates the body in that environment extended with the argument. This gives *lexical scope*: free names refer to the bindings visible where the function was written. If a function instead used the environment at the call site (*dynamic scope*), a later rebinding of `x` would change what an old function means.

The program below defines `f` using `x = 1`, rebinds `x` to 10, then calls `f 2`. Lexical scope gives `3` because the closure remembers `x = 1`; dynamic scope gives `12`. Almost every modern language, OCaml included, is lexically scoped, because it makes a function's behaviour depend only on its own text and its definition site.
code:
type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Var of string
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr
  | Fun of string * expr
  | App of expr * expr

type value = VInt of int | Closure of string * expr * (string * value) list

let show = function VInt n -> string_of_int n | Closure _ -> "<closure>"

let rec eval_lex env = function
  | Int n -> VInt n
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Add (a, b) -> (
      let x = eval_lex env a in
      let y = eval_lex env b in
      match (x, y) with VInt x, VInt y -> VInt (x + y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval_lex ((x, eval_lex env e1) :: env) e2
  | Fun (x, body) -> Closure (x, body, env)
  | App (f, arg) -> (
      match eval_lex env f with
      | Closure (x, body, closure_env) -> eval_lex ((x, eval_lex env arg) :: closure_env) body
      | _ -> failwith "not a function")

(* Dynamic scope: a function does not remember where it was defined. *)
let rec eval_dyn env = function
  | Int n -> VInt n
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Add (a, b) -> (
      let x = eval_dyn env a in
      let y = eval_dyn env b in
      match (x, y) with VInt x, VInt y -> VInt (x + y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval_dyn ((x, eval_dyn env e1) :: env) e2
  | Fun (x, body) -> Closure (x, body, [])
  | App (f, arg) -> (
      match eval_dyn env f with
      | Closure (x, body, _) -> eval_dyn ((x, eval_dyn env arg) :: env) body
      | _ -> failwith "not a function")

let () =
  let prog =
    Let ("x", Int 1,
         Let ("f", Fun ("y", Add (Var "x", Var "y")),
              Let ("x", Int 10, App (Var "f", Int 2))))
  in
  Printf.printf "lexical: %s\n" (show (eval_lex [] prog));
  Printf.printf "dynamic: %s\n" (show (eval_dyn [] prog));
  Printf.printf "a function value: %s\n" (show (eval_lex [] (Fun ("z", Var "z"))));
  try ignore (eval_lex [] (Var "missing")) with Not_found -> print_endline "unbound variable"
expectedStdout:
lexical: 3
dynamic: 12
a function value: <closure>
unbound variable
challenge: Evaluate `let add = fun a -> fun b -> a + b in (add 3) 4` with `eval_lex` to show that a closure can return another closure, and print the result.
solution:
type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Var of string
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr
  | Fun of string * expr
  | App of expr * expr

type value = VInt of int | Closure of string * expr * (string * value) list

let rec eval env = function
  | Int n -> VInt n
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Add (a, b) -> (
      let x = eval env a in
      let y = eval env b in
      match (x, y) with VInt x, VInt y -> VInt (x + y) | _ -> failwith "type error")
  | Let (x, e1, e2) -> eval ((x, eval env e1) :: env) e2
  | Fun (x, body) -> Closure (x, body, env)
  | App (f, arg) -> (
      match eval env f with
      | Closure (x, body, closure_env) -> eval ((x, eval env arg) :: closure_env) body
      | _ -> failwith "not a function")

let () =
  let prog =
    Let ("add", Fun ("a", Fun ("b", Add (Var "a", Var "b"))), App (App (Var "add", Int 3), Int 4))
  in
  match eval [] prog with VInt n -> Printf.printf "%d\n" n | Closure _ -> print_endline "closure"
question: Why does lexical scope give 3 in the example while dynamic scope gives 12?
correct: The closure remembers x = 1 from where f was defined; dynamic scope uses x = 10 from the call site
wrong: Dynamic scope ignores the argument y
reasoning: A closure carries its defining environment, so rebinding x afterwards cannot change what the function refers to.

title: A static type checker
body: A type checker predicts, without running the program, what kind of value each expression will produce. For a small language with integers and booleans, `typeof env e` returns the type of `e` in the typing environment `env`, or an error explaining the problem. `Add` needs two integers and gives an integer, `Le` compares integers and gives a boolean, and `If` needs a boolean condition and two branches of the same type.

The environment maps each variable to its type, extended at every `let`. An unbound variable is a type error. The result type is `(ty, string) result`, and `let*` threads the first error out, so the checker reads as the typing rules do: check the parts, then combine their types.

The point is *safety*: a well-typed program never gets stuck. Adding an integer to a boolean would stick the evaluator from the substitution lesson, and the checker rejects it first with a message. Type checking is conservative: it rejects some programs that would have run fine, and the art of a type system is rejecting as few useful programs as possible.
code:
type ty = TInt | TBool

type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Bool of bool
  | Var of string
  | Add of expr * expr
  | Le of expr * expr
  | If of expr * expr * expr
  | Let of string * expr * expr

let show_ty = function TInt -> "int" | TBool -> "bool"
let ( let* ) = Result.bind

let rec typeof env = function
  | Int _ -> Ok TInt
  | Bool _ -> Ok TBool
  | Var x -> (match List.assoc_opt x env with Some t -> Ok t | None -> Error ("unbound variable " ^ x))
  | Add (a, b) ->
      let* () = expect env a TInt in
      let* () = expect env b TInt in
      Ok TInt
  | Le (a, b) ->
      let* () = expect env a TInt in
      let* () = expect env b TInt in
      Ok TBool
  | If (c, t, f) ->
      let* () = expect env c TBool in
      let* tt = typeof env t in
      let* tf = typeof env f in
      if tt = tf then Ok tt else Error "branches differ"
  | Let (x, e1, e2) ->
      let* t1 = typeof env e1 in
      typeof ((x, t1) :: env) e2

and expect env e t =
  let* t' = typeof env e in
  if t' = t then Ok () else Error (Printf.sprintf "expected %s but got %s" (show_ty t) (show_ty t'))

let report e = print_endline (match typeof [] e with Ok t -> show_ty t | Error m -> "error: " ^ m)

let () =
  report (Add (Int 1, Int 2));
  report (If (Le (Int 1, Int 2), Int 3, Int 4));
  report (Let ("x", Bool true, If (Var "x", Int 1, Int 2)));
  report (Add (Int 1, Bool true));
  report (If (Int 1, Int 2, Int 3));
  report (If (Bool true, Int 1, Bool false));
  report (Var "z")
expectedStdout:
int
int
int
error: expected int but got bool
error: expected bool but got int
error: branches differ
error: unbound variable z
challenge: Add a `Not of expr` constructor to the language, type it as bool to bool, and report the type of `Not (Le (Int 1, Int 2))` and the error for `Not (Int 3)`.
solution:
type ty = TInt | TBool
type expr = Int of int | Le of expr * expr | Not of expr

let show_ty = function TInt -> "int" | TBool -> "bool"
let ( let* ) = Result.bind

let rec typeof = function
  | Int _ -> Ok TInt
  | Le (a, b) ->
      let* () = expect a TInt in
      let* () = expect b TInt in
      Ok TBool
  | Not e ->
      let* () = expect e TBool in
      Ok TBool

and expect e t =
  let* t' = typeof e in
  if t' = t then Ok () else Error (Printf.sprintf "expected %s but got %s" (show_ty t) (show_ty t'))

let report e = print_endline (match typeof e with Ok t -> show_ty t | Error m -> "error: " ^ m)

let () =
  report (Not (Le (Int 1, Int 2)));
  report (Not (Int 3))
solutionStdout:
bool
error: expected bool but got int
question: What guarantee does a sound type system give about a well-typed program?
correct: It never gets stuck: evaluation either finishes with a value or keeps making progress
reasoning: Soundness means progress and preservation: a well-typed term either is a value or can step, and stepping keeps its type.

title: Type inference by unification
body: A checker needs annotations; an inferencer discovers the types. It gives every unknown a fresh *type variable*, walks the expression generating constraints, and solves them by *unification*. Applying a function `f : a` to an argument of type `b` with result type `c` demands that `a` equal `b -> c`. Unification makes two types equal by binding type variables, or fails with a mismatch.

Unifying a variable with a type must pass the *occurs check*: a variable cannot be bound to a type that contains it, since that would be an infinite type. This is why `fun x -> x x` is rejected: `x` would need the type `a` with `a = a -> b`. The substitution built up during inference is applied at the end, and leftover variables are printed as `'a`, `'b` and so on, which are exactly the polymorphic types of OCaml.

This is the heart of Hindley-Milner inference, the system behind OCaml, with let-polymorphism omitted here for brevity. Note how the printer names variables in the order they appear and sequences its work with `let`, since the order of evaluation of arguments is unspecified and would otherwise change the names.
code:
type ty = TInt | TBool | TVar of int | TFun of ty * ty

type expr =
  | Int of int
  | Bool of bool
  | Var of string
  | Fun of string * expr
  | App of expr * expr
  | Add of expr * expr
  | If of expr * expr * expr

exception Type_error of string

let counter = ref 0
let subst : (int * ty) list ref = ref []
let fresh () = incr counter; TVar !counter

let rec resolve t =
  match t with
  | TVar n -> (match List.assoc_opt n !subst with Some t' -> resolve t' | None -> t)
  | TFun (a, b) -> TFun (resolve a, resolve b)
  | TInt | TBool -> t

let rec occurs n t =
  match resolve t with
  | TVar m -> n = m
  | TFun (a, b) -> occurs n a || occurs n b
  | TInt | TBool -> false

let rec unify a b =
  match (resolve a, resolve b) with
  | TInt, TInt | TBool, TBool -> ()
  | TVar n, TVar m when n = m -> ()
  | TVar n, t | t, TVar n ->
      if occurs n t then raise (Type_error "occurs check: infinite type") else subst := (n, t) :: !subst
  | TFun (a1, b1), TFun (a2, b2) -> unify a1 a2; unify b1 b2
  | _ -> raise (Type_error "type mismatch")

let rec infer env = function
  | Int _ -> TInt
  | Bool _ -> TBool
  | Var x -> (match List.assoc_opt x env with Some t -> t | None -> raise (Type_error ("unbound variable " ^ x)))
  | Fun (x, body) ->
      let a = fresh () in
      let r = infer ((x, a) :: env) body in
      TFun (a, r)
  | App (f, arg) ->
      let tf = infer env f in
      let ta = infer env arg in
      let r = fresh () in
      unify tf (TFun (ta, r));
      r
  | Add (a, b) -> unify (infer env a) TInt; unify (infer env b) TInt; TInt
  | If (c, t, e) ->
      unify (infer env c) TBool;
      let tt = infer env t in
      let te = infer env e in
      unify tt te;
      tt

let show t =
  let names = ref [] in
  let name n =
    match List.assoc_opt n !names with
    | Some s -> s
    | None ->
        let s = "'" ^ String.make 1 (Char.chr (97 + List.length !names)) in
        names := (n, s) :: !names;
        s
  in
  let rec go t =
    match resolve t with
    | TInt -> "int"
    | TBool -> "bool"
    | TVar n -> name n
    | TFun (a, b) ->
        let left = match resolve a with TFun _ -> "(" ^ go a ^ ")" | _ -> go a in
        let right = go b in
        left ^ " -> " ^ right
  in
  go t

let typeof e =
  counter := 0;
  subst := [];
  match infer [] e with t -> show t | exception Type_error m -> "error: " ^ m

let () =
  List.iter (fun e -> print_endline (typeof e))
    [ Fun ("x", Add (Var "x", Int 1));
      Fun ("x", Var "x");
      Fun ("f", Fun ("x", App (Var "f", App (Var "f", Var "x"))));
      Fun ("x", App (Var "x", Var "x"));
      If (Bool true, Int 1, Bool false);
      App (Int 1, Int 2) ]
expectedStdout:
int -> int
'a -> 'a
('a -> 'a) -> 'a -> 'a
error: occurs check: infinite type
error: type mismatch
error: type mismatch
challenge: Infer the type of the composition function `fun f -> fun g -> fun x -> f (g x)` by adding it to the list in a small program using the same inference code, and print it.
solution:
type ty = TInt | TBool | TVar of int | TFun of ty * ty
type expr = Var of string | Fun of string * expr | App of expr * expr

exception Type_error of string

let counter = ref 0
let subst : (int * ty) list ref = ref []
let fresh () = incr counter; TVar !counter

let rec resolve t =
  match t with
  | TVar n -> (match List.assoc_opt n !subst with Some t' -> resolve t' | None -> t)
  | TFun (a, b) -> TFun (resolve a, resolve b)
  | TInt | TBool -> t

let rec occurs n t =
  match resolve t with
  | TVar m -> n = m
  | TFun (a, b) -> occurs n a || occurs n b
  | TInt | TBool -> false

let rec unify a b =
  match (resolve a, resolve b) with
  | TInt, TInt | TBool, TBool -> ()
  | TVar n, TVar m when n = m -> ()
  | TVar n, t | t, TVar n ->
      if occurs n t then raise (Type_error "occurs check") else subst := (n, t) :: !subst
  | TFun (a1, b1), TFun (a2, b2) -> unify a1 a2; unify b1 b2
  | _ -> raise (Type_error "mismatch")

let rec infer env = function
  | Var x -> List.assoc x env
  | Fun (x, body) ->
      let a = fresh () in
      let r = infer ((x, a) :: env) body in
      TFun (a, r)
  | App (f, arg) ->
      let tf = infer env f in
      let ta = infer env arg in
      let r = fresh () in
      unify tf (TFun (ta, r));
      r

let show t =
  let names = ref [] in
  let name n =
    match List.assoc_opt n !names with
    | Some s -> s
    | None ->
        let s = "'" ^ String.make 1 (Char.chr (97 + List.length !names)) in
        names := (n, s) :: !names;
        s
  in
  let rec go t =
    match resolve t with
    | TInt -> "int"
    | TBool -> "bool"
    | TVar n -> name n
    | TFun (a, b) ->
        let left = match resolve a with TFun _ -> "(" ^ go a ^ ")" | _ -> go a in
        let right = go b in
        left ^ " -> " ^ right
  in
  go t

let () =
  let compose = Fun ("f", Fun ("g", Fun ("x", App (Var "f", App (Var "g", Var "x"))))) in
  print_endline (show (infer [] compose))
question: Why is `fun x -> x x` rejected by inference?
correct: Unifying x with x -> r would give a type that contains itself, which the occurs check forbids
wrong: Because x is not a function
Because the argument x is unbound
reasoning: The constraint a = a -> r has no finite solution, so the occurs check raises an error before binding the variable.

title: The Curry-Howard correspondence: programs as proofs
body: A type can be read as a proposition and a program of that type as a proof of it. A function type `A -> B` is the implication 'if A then B', a pair `A * B` is 'A and B', and `(A, B) Either.t` is 'A or B'. A *total* function of type `A -> B` turns any evidence for A into evidence for B, which is exactly what a proof of an implication does.

So `compose : (a -> b) -> (b -> c) -> (a -> c)` is the transitivity of implication, and `and_comm : a * b -> b * a` proves that 'and' is commutative. The empty type `type void = |` has no values, so it plays the role of falsehood, and `a -> void` is 'not a'. From `a` you can prove 'not not a' by applying the continuation to it, but you cannot prove 'not not a implies a' in general: that classical principle has no program.

OCaml is not sound as a logic. Non-termination (`let rec loop () = loop ()`), exceptions and `Obj.magic` all inhabit any type, so a type-correct program is evidence only when it is total and pure. The correspondence is nevertheless the foundation of proof assistants such as Lean and Coq, where the type system is restricted until programs really are proofs.

5
one 1
right 7
5
42
1 x
all propositions type-check
challenge: Prove, by writing a function with the type, that `(a -> b -> c) -> (b -> a -> c)` (swapping arguments), and print `swap_args (-) 10 3` after applying it to integer subtraction.
solution:
let swap_args (f : 'a -> 'b -> 'c) : 'b -> 'a -> 'c = fun b a -> f a b

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (swap_args ( - ) 10 3)
question: In the Curry-Howard reading, what does a value of type `a -> void` stand for?
correct: A proof that a is false, since it turns any evidence for a into the impossible
wrong: A proof that a is true
A program that never returns a value
reasoning: The empty type has no values, so a function into it can only exist if its argument type has none either.

title: Big-O notation measured by counting
body: Big-O describes how the cost of an algorithm grows with the size n of its input, ignoring constant factors. Linear search is O(n), binary search is O(log n), insertion sort is O(n squared), and merge sort is O(n log n). The notation answers one question: if I double the input, what happens to the work?

You can see the growth rate by counting a basic operation instead of measuring time. Count the comparisons in each algorithm at sizes n and 2n. A linear algorithm doubles its count, a logarithmic one adds a constant, a quadratic one quadruples, and an n log n algorithm slightly more than doubles. Counts are exact and repeatable, where timings depend on the machine and the load.

Big-O is an upper bound on growth, not a prediction of speed. An O(n squared) algorithm with a tiny constant can beat an O(n log n) one for small inputs, and the worst case may be rare. Use the notation to choose the right algorithm family, then measure to decide among the contenders.
expectedStdout:
linear doubles: true
binary search adds one step: true
insertion sort roughly quadruples: true
merge sort slightly more than doubles: true
challenge: Count the comparisons made by `List.mem` style linear search over lists of 100 and 200 elements for an absent value and print the two counts.
question: What happens to the work of a quadratic algorithm when the input doubles?
wrong: It increases by a constant amount
reasoning: Work proportional to n squared becomes proportional to (2n) squared, which is four times as much.
